title: Stop before the extra iteration
summary: Use a breakpoint to find a loop that includes one reading beyond its count.
objectives: Pause before a repeated load and compare its index with the count.
Repair an off-by-one test and check the empty case.
before: The trip computer must add the first t0 unsigned bytes in lesson_data. Valid indices stop before the count. The starting loop allows an extra iteration. The following byte is still readable, so a successful run does not establish that the loop used the right elements.

A breakpoint pauses execution before a chosen machine instruction. Open Debugger, then click the source line number beside lbu to mark that load. Start debugging builds a fresh machine and runs to the breakpoint. The marked line has not executed when the machine pauses.

A watch keeps a value visible while you investigate. In Debugger, choose a Register and use Pin register. Pin t0, t2 and t3 to watch the count, index and byte address. Continue reaches the next selected breakpoint or code end. Compare index and count at each pause. Step instruction executes one machine instruction.
Predict the final a0 from the faulty program as written. Then pause at the load and find the first iteration that should not run.
starter:
la t1, lesson_data
li t2, 0
li a0, 0
scan_readings:
    bltu t0, t2, readings_done
    add t3, t1, t2
    lbu t4, 0(t3)
    add a0, a0, t4
    addi t2, t2, 1
    j scan_readings
readings_done:

prediction.prompt: What does a0 hold after the faulty starting loop finishes?
prediction.hint: Follow the branch with index equal to the count. Does it leave the loop before loading?

explanation: An off-by-one error runs an operation once too often or once too few. Here the branch leaves only when the count is less than the index. Equality therefore reaches the load, although an index equal to the count already lies beyond the requested elements.

The breakpoint makes the order visible. At each pause, the branch and address calculation have run, but the load has not. The index and address explain which byte the next step will read. The final total alone cannot identify which iteration introduced the error.

Repair the stopping condition before changing the arithmetic. An unsigned index must leave when it is greater than or equal to the unsigned count. Starting from zero also needs to leave immediately for an empty input. A zero count is a useful check because the faulty first load then has no valid reading to represent.

experiment.task: After `la t1, lesson_data`, insert `li t5, 9` followed by `sb t5, 3(t1)`. Keep the count in t0 unchanged. Run the faulty loop and note a0 in Registers. Remove the two inserted instructions and run again. Then repair the stopping test and repeat that pair of runs. Should changing a byte outside the requested range affect the corrected total?
experiment.hint: The data cells display bytes; they do not edit them. The explicit store changes byte offset three. A total for the first t0 bytes must not depend on that byte.

challenge.task: Repair the loop so a0 is the sum of exactly the first t0 unsigned bytes in lesson_data. The supplied count is between 0 and 63. Leave t2 equal to the number of bytes included. Do not read an element when its index equals the count.
challenge.starter:
la t1, lesson_data
li t2, 0
li a0, 0
scan_readings:
    bltu t0, t2, readings_done
    add t3, t1, t2
    lbu t4, 0(t3)
    add a0, a0, t4
    addi t2, t2, 1
    j scan_readings
readings_done:
challenge.reference:
la t1, lesson_data
li t2, 0
li a0, 0
scan_readings:
    bgeu t2, t0, readings_done
    add t3, t1, t2
    lbu t4, 0(t3)
    add a0, a0, t4
    addi t2, t2, 1
    j scan_readings
readings_done:
hints: At the load breakpoint, compare the index with the count before reading the byte.
The stopping branch must accept equality. Think about which operand is the index in bgeu.
For zero readings, the first branch must skip every load and leave the total and index at zero.

cases.name: One reading and a different following byte

originalityNote: Use the trip computer’s bounded byte sum to investigate a readable extra element with repeated real breakpoints instead of treating a final wrong total as the whole explanation.

title: Find the wrong byte reading
summary: Watch a loaded sensor byte before a later multiplication hides where its signed reading began.
objectives: Distinguish the byte in memory from the register pattern produced by a load.
Locate and repair an incorrect sign-extending load.
before: The trip computer stores a pulse count as one unsigned byte and multiplies it by the scale in t0. The starting program loads the byte with lb. That instruction copies bit 7 into the register’s upper bits. A byte whose top bit is one therefore becomes a negative signed register reading.

To find where the wrong reading enters, set a breakpoint by clicking the source line number beside mul. Start debugging pauses before that multiplication; the load has already run. Pin t2 in Debugger and compare its full register pattern with byte offset zero in Memory.

The low eight register bits can match the memory byte even when the full register reading is wrong for the task. Inspect the upper bits and the signed and unsigned register readings. The request describes an unsigned byte, so the instruction choice must preserve that meaning when widening it.

Predict a0 after the faulty program completes, then use Step instruction or Continue to compare the multiplication with the loaded value you observed. The watch displays captured machine state; changing a decimal reading does not execute another load.
starter:
la t1, lesson_data
lb t2, 0(t1)
mul a0, t2, t0

prediction.prompt: What signed value does a0 hold after the starting lb and multiplication?
prediction.hint: Read the byte as lb defines it, then multiply that signed reading by the scale.

explanation: The multiplication receives a full 64-bit pattern. It cannot tell whether that pattern came from a signed sample or an unsigned count. Changing the result’s display to unsigned also cannot repair the value that the load supplied.

lbu fills the upper register bits with zeros. That choice gives a one-byte unsigned count the intended wider reading. A small test whose byte has bit 7 clear can conceal the mistake because lb and lbu then produce the same register pattern.

The useful debugging pause is between the load and its consumer. First establish the memory byte, then the loaded register, then the scaled result. This order separates a bad input reading from a multiplication error and gives the repair a specific reason.

experiment.task: Replace `lb t2, 0(t1)` with `lbu t2, 0(t1)`. Edits clear breakpoints, so mark mul again and choose Start debugging. Compare the paused t2 pattern in Debugger. Then insert `li t3, 7` and `sb t3, 0(t1)` immediately after `la t1, lesson_data`. Compare lb with lbu on that byte, marking mul again after each edit. Keep the scale in t0 unchanged.
experiment.hint: The explicit store changes the input byte; the data cells are read-only. Keep the scale unchanged. Only the load’s extension of that byte should differ between the two instruction choices.

challenge.task: Repair the unsigned sensor-byte load. Return in a0 the low 64 bits of the unsigned byte at lesson_data multiplied by the unsigned scale in t0. The byte and scale are supplied by each case.
challenge.starter:
la t1, lesson_data
lb t2, 0(t1)
mul a0, t2, t0
challenge.reference:
la t1, lesson_data
lbu t2, 0(t1)
mul a0, t2, t0
hints: Pause before mul and inspect t2 before changing the multiplication.
The byte is unsigned. Select the byte load that clears the upper register bits.
A byte with bit 7 clear does not distinguish lb from lbu. Check a case with that bit set.

originalityNote: Investigate a real unsigned sensor byte at the load-to-multiply boundary so the debugger exposes extension before later arithmetic carries the wrong pattern forward.

title: Follow the saved return address
summary: Inspect a helper’s stack slot and find why a nested call can return to the wrong instruction.
objectives: Observe ra before and after a nested call.
Restore the saved return address and release the same stack frame.
before: The starting program works: add_service doubles a0 through scale_ticks, then adds a service allowance. The outer helper must keep its caller’s return address while the nested call writes a new one into ra. The editor shows the save and restore.

Open Debugger and mark the line containing `call scale_ticks`. Choose Start debugging to pause before that call. Pin ra and sp, then open Inspect the stack within Debugger. The earlier `sd ra, 8(sp)` has stored the outer return address at sp + 8.

Stack inspection shows observed addresses and bytes. A stored number becomes a saved return address because this code put ra there; the debugger does not infer a complete chain of callers. One source call can expand into several machine instructions. Use Step instruction until execution enters scale_ticks, and compare ra with the saved slot.

Predict a0 when the working example returns. The optional exercise removes the save and restore. Use Start debugging and Step instruction, then Stop when you understand the repeated return. Repair the code before Check all cases; otherwise it can run until the execution limit.
starter:
call add_service
j service_done
add_service:
    addi sp, sp, -16
    sd ra, 8(sp)
    call scale_ticks
    addi a0, a0, 3
    ld ra, 8(sp)
    addi sp, sp, 16
    ret
scale_ticks:
    slli a0, a0, 1
    ret
service_done:

prediction.prompt: What does a0 hold when the working starting example reaches service_done?
prediction.hint: Follow the value returned by scale_ticks, then the addition in add_service.

explanation: A call writes a return destination into ra. The inner ret uses that destination to resume add_service. The outer ret must instead use the address that was in ra before the inner call. Keeping the two destinations separate is part of making nested calls work.

Without the restore, the outer ret selects the continuation inside add_service again. That can repeat the allowance and stack release instead of reaching service_done. A changing result or stack pointer is evidence of those repeated instructions, not evidence that ret returns the value in a0.

The working frame reserves sixteen bytes and releases the same amount. Its saved ra occupies offset eight. Inspect that slot while the frame is active; after release, the current sp names a different area. The optional exercise checks the returned value and preservation of the prepared initial sp.

experiment.task: Mark `call scale_ticks` and `ld ra, 8(sp)` as breakpoints in the working example. Choose Start debugging, then Continue to reach the second pause. In Debugger, compare ra with the saved slot at byte offset eight in Inspect the stack at both pauses. sp still names the same outer frame.
experiment.hint: The stack bytes can keep the outer return address while ra holds the inner return destination. Follow both locations across the call.

challenge.task: Repair add_service so it doubles the supplied a0, adds 3 and returns to service_done. Save its incoming ra before calling scale_ticks and restore that saved address afterwards. Preserve the starting sp. Keep scale_ticks as the nested helper.
challenge.starter:
call add_service
j service_done
add_service:
    addi sp, sp, -16
    call scale_ticks
    addi a0, a0, 3
    addi sp, sp, 16
    ret
scale_ticks:
    slli a0, a0, 1
    ret
service_done:
challenge.reference:
call add_service
j service_done
add_service:
    addi sp, sp, -16
    sd ra, 8(sp)
    call scale_ticks
    addi a0, a0, 3
    ld ra, 8(sp)
    addi sp, sp, 16
    ret
scale_ticks:
    slli a0, a0, 1
    ret
service_done:
hints: The nested call overwrites ra before add_service has returned to its own caller.
The sixteen-byte frame has space for the incoming return address. Save it before the nested call and load that same slot afterwards.
Restore ra while sp still names the frame, then release exactly sixteen bytes before the outer ret.

originalityNote: Use a trip service helper and a specific observed ra slot to diagnose nested-return repetition, with stack preservation checked from the executed program rather than an invented call-stack diagram.

title: Stop an access before it leaves the range
summary: Separate a readable address from an element that belongs to the requested byte range.
objectives: Inspect a computed address before its load executes.
Place a range check before the access and test the protected boundary.
before: The requested range begins at lesson_data and contains t1 bytes. The offset in t0 is valid only below that count. The starting code loads immediately, without checking. Its supplied offset lies beyond the logical range but still in readable memory.

Set a breakpoint on lbu and choose Start debugging. Pin t0, t1 and t3 to compare the offset, count and computed address before the load. A readable byte need not belong to the requested range. Predict t2 from the faulty load, then inspect the supplied byte at that offset.

A page is a block of memory with its own access permissions. The lab places its sixty-four data bytes immediately before a page protected from this xv6 user process. A forbidden access causes a fault: xv6 stops the process before it can report completed state. Output → xv6 serial log records that failure.

The optional exercise loads first and repairs the returned value afterwards. Pause before its load and inspect the order. A later check cannot undo an access. Repair that order before running the protected-boundary case.
starter:
la t3, lesson_data
add t3, t3, t0
lbu t2, 0(t3)

prediction.prompt: What signed value does t2 hold after the unchecked starting load?
prediction.hint: Compute the byte offset literally. The starting code has no branch that skips the load.

explanation: Memory protection controls which addresses the process can access. Your logical bound decides which elements belong to this operation. Reading an extra accessible byte may succeed while still using a value outside the requested input.

The corrected order first prepares the invalid-offset result, then branches around address calculation and loading when the offset is outside the count. Every executed load is reached through the valid path. Unsigned comparison also rejects offsets whose register patterns have their high bit set.

The boundary case distinguishes skipping a load from repairing its result. When offset and count both equal sixty-four, equality must leave before loading the protected following page. A failed access has no completed snapshot. Inspect the serial log and last paused address instead of treating a missing report as a numerical result.

experiment.task: Insert `li t0, 1` at the start of the example. Mark lbu and choose Start debugging to inspect t3 before the load. Repeat with `li t0, 3`, equal to the supplied count, and stop before loading. For the guarded version, place `li t2, -1` and `bgeu t0, t1, range_done` after the new li but before la. Add `range_done:` after lbu. Run each offset again and compare t2 in Registers: the invalid path must skip the load.
experiment.hint: Change t0 through the source instruction; Starting inputs shows the supplied value before that instruction runs. In Debugger, Add memory watch with Base lesson_data, Byte offset 3 and Width 1 byte keeps the extra byte visible. Check the protected-boundary case only after correcting the exercise code.

challenge.task: Repair the access order. t0 is an unsigned byte offset and t1 is an unsigned capacity from 0 to 64. If offset is below capacity, load the unsigned byte at lesson_data + offset into t2. Otherwise leave t2 = -1 and do not perform the load.
challenge.starter:
la t3, lesson_data
add t3, t3, t0
lbu t2, 0(t3)
bltu t0, t1, range_done
li t2, -1
range_done:
challenge.reference:
li t2, -1
bgeu t0, t1, range_done
la t3, lesson_data
add t3, t3, t0
lbu t2, 0(t3)
range_done:
hints: Changing t2 after a load cannot make the earlier access safe.
Prepare -1, then branch over address calculation and loading when the unsigned offset is greater than or equal to capacity.
Equality at capacity sixty-four reaches a protected page if you load first. The comparison must execute before that load.

cases.name: Readable but outside the logical range

originalityNote: Use both a readable extra byte and xv6’s actual protected following page to distinguish a trip record’s logical range from memory protection and to expose a load performed before its check.
